choking-what-the-nhs-and-resus-council-d.name: Choking in adults and children: what to do
choking-what-the-nhs-and-resus-council-d.headline: Choking in adults, children and babies: what first-aid guidance describes
choking-what-the-nhs-and-resus-council-d.summary: First-aid guidance describes back blows and abdominal thrusts for severe choking, 999 if the blockage stays, and a medical check after abdominal thrusts.
keyPoints: Mild choking is described as being able to speak, cough or breathe, and encouraging the person to keep coughing is the advice.
Severe choking is described as being unable to speak, cough or breathe, and the person may become unconscious without help.
For adults, first-aid sources describe up to five back blows, then up to five abdominal thrusts, repeated in turn.
Babies under one are described as having back blows and chest thrusts, never abdominal thrusts.
Anyone treated with abdominal thrusts or chest thrusts is described as needing a check by a health professional afterwards.

body.heading: How can mild and severe choking be told apart?
body.body:
First-aid guidance describes mild choking as a person who can still speak, cough or breathe. Such a person can usually clear the blockage alone, and the advice is to encourage them to keep coughing. The Resuscitation Council UK advises against blind finger sweeps of the mouth, because they can push the object further back.

Severe choking is described as being unable to speak, cough or breathe. Without help, the person eventually becomes unconscious. First-aid guidance only moves to back blows when coughing is not possible or is not working.

body.heading: What do first-aid sources describe for a choking adult?
body.body:
NHS inform describes leaning the person well forward and giving up to five sharp blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of the hand. If the blockage remains, it describes abdominal thrusts, with a clenched fist placed between the navel and the bottom of the breastbone, gripped with the other hand and pulled sharply inwards and upwards. This is repeated up to five times.

The British Red Cross gives the same order of steps for an adult: encourage coughing, then up to five back blows, then up to five abdominal thrusts. The Resuscitation Council UK 2025 guidance describes alternating five back blows with five abdominal thrusts until the choking is relieved or the person becomes unresponsive. For a pregnant person, the Resuscitation Council UK says abdominal thrusts are not performed, and the hands are placed higher, over the lower end of the breastbone.

body.heading: When is 999 called, and what if the person stops responding?
body.body:
NHS inform describes calling 999 if the blockage has not cleared, then repeating the back blows and abdominal thrusts while waiting for help. The Resuscitation Council UK describes calling 999 once choking has not been relieved after the first five abdominal thrusts. The British Red Cross says to call 999 if the person is still choking. St John Ambulance describes calling 999 or 112 for a baby or child if the blockage has not cleared. The wording on timing differs a little between sources, but each links the call to a blockage that has not cleared.

If the person becomes unresponsive, the Resuscitation Council UK describes starting CPR and making sure 999 has been called. NHS inform describes opening the airway, checking breathing, and starting CPR if the person is not breathing.

body.heading: How does choking in a baby under one differ?
body.body:
The NHS describes up to five sharp back blows, with the baby lying face down along the thigh or forearm and the head kept low. If the blockage stays, the NHS describes up to five chest thrusts, with the baby face up and two fingers placed in the middle of the chest, just below the nipple line. The NHS describes checking the mouth between each blow or thrust.

Abdominal thrusts are not used on babies under one year old. The NHS says to call 999 if the object does not come out, and to keep alternating back blows and chest thrusts until help arrives. If the baby becomes unconscious, it describes calling 999 and starting CPR. The Resuscitation Council UK likewise describes back blows and chest thrusts rather than abdominal thrusts for infants. The NHS also advises against finger sweeps, which can push the object further back.

body.heading: What changes for a child over one?
body.body:
The NHS pairs back blows with abdominal thrusts for children over one. It describes a clenched fist placed between the navel and the ribs, pulled sharply inwards and upwards, repeated up to five times, checking after each whether the object has come out. If the blockage does not clear after back blows and abdominal thrusts, the NHS describes calling 999 and continuing the cycle until help arrives.

The British Red Cross describes continuing cycles of back blows and abdominal thrusts until the object comes out, help arrives or the child becomes unresponsive. St John Ambulance describes starting child CPR if the child becomes unresponsive. For children, the Resuscitation Council UK paediatric guidance describes up to five back blows if coughing is not possible or is becoming ineffective, followed by thrusts.

body.heading: Is a medical check needed afterwards?
body.body:
The NHS says that even when the object comes out, medical help is advised, because part of the object may remain or the child may have been hurt by the procedure. The Resuscitation Council UK gives a similar reason for adults, saying that complications and injuries can occur after abdominal thrusts or chest compressions, so a healthcare professional should see anyone treated this way.

St John Ambulance says that every baby who has had chest thrusts, and every child who has had abdominal thrusts, should be seen in hospital, even if the blockage has cleared.

The Resuscitation Council UK published new first-aid guidelines in October 2025, so its current pages are the reference if details change.

references.title: NHS inform: Adult choking first aid
NHS: How to stop a child from choking
Resuscitation Council UK: First aid guidelines 2025
British Red Cross: Choking first aid advice for an adult

travel-vaccinations-what-the-nhs-says.name: Which travel vaccinations might be needed?
travel-vaccinations-what-the-nhs-says.headline: Travel vaccinations: what the NHS says about which are needed and when to arrange them
travel-vaccinations-what-the-nhs-says.summary: The NHS advises getting travel vaccine advice several weeks before departure, as needs depend on the destination, and some vaccines are free while others are paid for.
keyPoints: The NHS advises seeing a GP practice, pharmacy or private travel clinic well ahead of a trip, because some vaccines need time to work or come as a course.
Which vaccines are advised depends on the countries visited, and TravelHealthPro lists the advice for each destination.
The NHS says some travel vaccines are free through the GP, including diphtheria, tetanus and polio, typhoid, hepatitis A and cholera, while others are usually paid for.
Yellow fever vaccination is given only at designated centres, is not free on the NHS, and leads to an international certificate.
Malaria is prevented with tablets rather than a travel vaccine, and the NHS advises getting advice from a GP, nurse, pharmacist or travel clinic before travel.
Pregnancy and health conditions can change which vaccines are suitable, so the NHS advises telling the person giving the vaccine.

body.heading: When should travel vaccinations be arranged?
body.body:
The NHS advises seeing a GP practice nurse or a private travel clinic well before a trip. Some vaccines need time to build protection, and some come as a course of several doses spread over weeks or months. The NHS travel vaccinations page gives around four to six weeks before departure.

Leaving it late is not a reason to skip the appointment. TravelHealthPro says some vaccines can still be given at the last minute, and malaria tablets can be started on the day of travel if needed. It adds that people who are pregnant or have a long-term condition may need to be seen earlier.

body.heading: Where can country-specific advice be found?
body.body:
Needs differ from one country to another. TravelHealthPro, run by the UK's National Travel Health Network and Centre, publishes country pages that list the vaccines and other health advice for each destination.

The NHS says a GP practice or travel clinic decides which vaccines are suitable and whether they can be given on the NHS.

body.heading: Which travel vaccines does the NHS list?
body.body:
The NHS lists several vaccines that may be advised for travel, depending on the destination. These include hepatitis A, typhoid, cholera, yellow fever, rabies, Japanese encephalitis, hepatitis B, tick-borne encephalitis, meningitis and tuberculosis (TB).

The NHS also lists the combined diphtheria, tetanus and polio vaccine among the vaccines relevant to travel.

body.heading: Which are free on the NHS and which are paid for?
body.body:
The NHS says some travel vaccines are free through a GP practice. These are the combined diphtheria, tetanus and polio vaccine, typhoid, hepatitis A and cholera.

Other travel vaccines are usually paid for. The NHS names hepatitis B, Japanese encephalitis, meningitis, rabies, tick-borne encephalitis, tuberculosis (TB) and yellow fever.

body.heading: What is the yellow fever certificate, and how is malaria prevented?
body.body:
The NHS says yellow fever vaccination is available only at designated centres and is not free on the NHS. It says the vaccine needs to be given at least 10 days before travel, and a checklist is used to confirm that a person can have it. A single dose is thought to give lifelong protection, and the certificate issued afterwards, the International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis, is valid for life.

Malaria is prevented with tablets rather than a travel vaccine. The NHS advises getting advice from a GP, nurse, pharmacist or travel clinic before travel, ideally four to six weeks ahead, though advice can still be sought at the last minute.

body.heading: What about pregnancy and long-term conditions?
body.body:
The NHS advises telling the person giving a travel vaccine about any health conditions or pregnancy, and bringing a list of any medicines.

In pregnancy, the NHS says to avoid areas where yellow fever is common where possible. It lists yellow fever among the live vaccines not usually advised in pregnancy, but says it may be considered necessary when travelling to areas where yellow fever is common, because the risks of the illness are so high. The NHS advises anyone unsure to talk to a midwife or GP about the risks and benefits.

head-injury-and-concussion-when-to-get-h.name: Head injury and concussion: when to get help
head-injury-and-concussion-when-to-get-h.headline: What happens after a head injury, which signs need 999 or A&E, and how concussion usually settles
head-injury-and-concussion-when-to-get-h.summary: Most head injuries are not serious, but the NHS says being knocked out and not waking, a fit or being unable to stay awake need a 999 call.
keyPoints: The NHS says to call 999 if a person was knocked out and has not woken up, cannot stay awake or keep their eyes open, or has a fit (seizure).

NHS inform says to go to A&E or call 999 for repeated vomiting, a severe or worsening headache, increasing drowsiness or confusion; the NHS says to get help from NHS 111 if the person is being sick or feels dizzy.
NICE sets out when a CT head scan is advised in hospital, with separate rules for adults and for children under 16.
The NHS says someone should stay with the injured person for the first 24 hours; NHS inform describes a responsible adult watching for 72 hours when concussion is suspected.
Headway says fewer than one in ten concussions involve loss of consciousness, and that going back to sport too early risks a second blow before the brain has recovered.

body.heading: What counts as a head injury, and what is concussion?
body.body:
The NHS says most head injuries are not serious, but it advises getting medical help for any symptoms. Concussion is a temporary brain injury, and the NHS says it can last a few weeks.

Headway describes concussion as the brain shaking back and forth inside the skull, causing mild damage. Being knocked out is not required. Headway says fewer than one in ten concussions involve loss of consciousness.

Headway lists confusion, dizziness and forgetfulness after a significant blow to the head as early signs. It says headaches, poor concentration and sleep problems can appear over the following days.

body.heading: Which signs mean calling 999?
body.body:
The NHS head injury page says to call 999 if the person has been knocked out and has not woken up. It gives the same route if the person cannot stay awake or keep their eyes open, or has a fit (seizure).

The NHS also lists a fall from more than 1 metre or five stairs, problems with vision or hearing, clear fluid coming from the ears or nose, and bleeding or bruising behind the ears. NHS 111 Wales adds numbness or weakness in part of the body, and problems with walking, balance, understanding or speaking.

NHS 111 Wales also says that 999 is the route if someone cannot be taken to A&E safely.

body.heading: When is A&E the route, and when NHS 111?
body.body:
NHS inform says to go to A&E or call 999 for repeated vomiting, a worsening or severe headache, increasing drowsiness or confusion. NHS 111 Wales lists A&E for a person who was knocked out but has since woken, has vomited since the injury, has a headache that painkillers do not ease, shows a change in behaviour or has memory problems.

The NHS says to get help from NHS 111 if the person is being sick or feels dizzy. NHS inform says that when concussion is suspected but there are no signs needing urgent A&E care, it advises phoning NHS 111 for advice, even if a hospital visit is not needed.

body.heading: What happens at A&E, and who has a CT scan?
body.body:
In hospital, staff assess the person after a head injury. NICE guidance, written for health professionals, covers assessment and early management and sets out when a CT head scan is advised.

For adults aged 16 and over, NICE advises a scan if the score on a standard alertness scale is still lower than normal two hours after the injury. A scan within eight hours is advised for people who were knocked out or have memory loss since the injury, and for people taking anticoagulant (blood-thinning) medicines.

For children under 16 the rules are separate. NICE also describes observing children for a minimum of four hours when no risk factors are present.

body.heading: What about babies and children?
body.body:
The advice comes from local NHS trust leaflets, which differ a little. Many describe an adult watching the child for 48 hours after a head injury, while some say 24 to 48 hours.

The leaflets list signs for 999 or A&E, including repeated vomiting (more than twice), becoming drowsy or hard to wake, confusion, a fit, difficulty speaking or understanding, weakness in the arms or legs, loss of balance, problems with eyesight, and clear fluid from the nose or ears. For babies they add not waking for feeds, or crying that cannot be soothed.

Some leaflets put a headache that does not go away in the 999 or A&E group, while Alder Hey places it under NHS 111 or an urgent GP review unless it is getting worse.

body.heading: What care at home does the NHS describe?
body.body:
The NHS says someone should stay with the injured person for the first 24 hours. NHS inform describes a responsible adult keeping watch for 72 hours when concussion is suspected, and says the person should not drive, drink alcohol, take recreational drugs or play sport.

NHS 111 Wales says a person who is tired does not need to stay awake. NHS inform describes a staged recovery plan, starting with relative rest for 24 to 48 hours and light activity with little screen time.

Trust leaflets differ on timings, so the advice from the treating team is the one that applies.

body.heading: What if symptoms carry on, and when can sport resume?
body.body:
Headway says to see a GP if symptoms persist. One of its leaflets gives about two weeks and another gives 28 days, and it says symptoms that are severe or getting worse need prompt medical assessment.

Headway advises against returning to play or training until cleared by a medical professional, even if the person feels fine, and describes a staged return to sport. It says another blow to the head before the brain has recovered can worsen the damage and, on rare occasions, can be fatal.

NHS inform's post-concussion syndrome page describes pacing, which means increasing activity gradually, to help with returning to work and leisure.

references.title: NHS 111 Wales: Head injury and concussion
NICE NG232: Head injury, assessment and early management
Alder Hey Children's Hospital: Head injury

heat-exhaustion-and-heatstroke-what-to-k.name: Heat exhaustion and heatstroke: what to know
heat-exhaustion-and-heatstroke-what-to-k.headline: Heat exhaustion and heatstroke: the difference, the signs, and when to call 999
heat-exhaustion-and-heatstroke-what-to-k.summary: Heat exhaustion usually eases with cooling and rest, while heatstroke is an emergency for which the NHS says to call 999.
keyPoints: Heat exhaustion can cause tiredness, dizziness, headache, feeling or being sick, heavy sweating, pale clammy skin and cramps.
Heatstroke is the more serious stage, with very hot skin that is not sweating, confusion, fast breathing, a fit or loss of consciousness.
For heat exhaustion the NHS describes moving somewhere cool, removing extra clothing, drinking water and cooling the skin.
The NHS says to call 999 if someone has not started to improve after 30 minutes of resting in a cool place, or if heatstroke is suspected.
Older people, babies and young children, and people with long-term conditions are described as most vulnerable in hot weather.

body.heading: What is the difference between heat exhaustion and heatstroke?
body.body:
Heat exhaustion happens when the body struggles to cope with heat. Heatstroke is the more serious form, and the NHS treats it as an emergency.

NHS inform says heat exhaustion can progress to heatstroke if a person cannot cool down. The NHS says heat exhaustion usually improves once the person cools down within 30 minutes, and NHS inform describes it as usually getting better 30 to 60 minutes after cooling. Someone who has heatstroke, NHS inform says, is treated in hospital.

body.heading: What are the signs of heat exhaustion?
body.body:
The NHS lists tiredness, dizziness, headache, feeling sick or being sick, and heavy sweating. The skin can become pale and clammy, and there can be cramps and a high temperature.

For children, the British Red Cross describes dizziness or confusion, headaches or cramps, sweating with cooler skin, a paler colour than usual, nausea, and fast breathing and heart rate. Its advice is to get medical advice even if the child seems to recover, and to call 999 if the child gets worse.

body.heading: What helps heat exhaustion?
body.body:
For heat exhaustion the NHS describes moving the person somewhere cool and taking off unnecessary clothing. It also describes giving plenty of water, or an isotonic sports drink or rehydration powder. The skin can be cooled by spraying or sponging with cool water and fanning. Cold packs wrapped in a cloth, placed under the armpits or on the neck, are also described. The NHS says to stay with the person until they are better.

The British Red Cross notes that babies under 6 months do not need to be offered water and may need to feed more often instead.

body.heading: What are the signs of heatstroke and what happens next?
body.body:
The NHS lists a very high temperature, and hot skin that is not sweating, among the warning signs of heatstroke. Others are fast breathing, a fast heartbeat, confusion, restlessness, a seizure (fit) and loss of consciousness. The NHS notes that redness can be harder to see on brown or black skin.

If heatstroke is suspected, the NHS says to call 999. It also says not to drive to A&E, and that the 999 call handler will advise what to do. The NHS also says to call 999 if someone with heat exhaustion has not begun to improve after 30 minutes of resting in a cool place, being cooled down and drinking fluids.

body.heading: What is done while waiting for help?
body.body:
The NHS describes cooling the person while waiting for the ambulance. This can mean wrapping them in a cool, wet sheet, fanning them, or sponging them with cold water. If the person loses consciousness, the NHS describes putting them in the recovery position. It also describes checking breathing and pulse and starting CPR if there is no sign of life.

For children, the British Red Cross likewise describes calling 999 straight away for heatstroke, moving the child somewhere cool and carrying on cooling while waiting for help.

body.heading: Who is at higher risk, and how can people stay cool?
body.body:
GOV.UK describes older people, babies and young children, and people with long-term conditions as more vulnerable in hot weather. Conditions named include heart, breathing and kidney problems and diabetes.

NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service guidance says some medicines may reduce sweating and affect the body's ability to control temperature, which can raise the risk of heat exhaustion and heatstroke. For staying cool, GOV.UK describes closing curtains or blinds on rooms facing the sun, and opening windows at night when it is cooler outside. It also describes planning activity for early morning or evening, drinking plenty of fluids, and limiting alcohol. Never leave babies, children, older people or pets alone in a parked car, the guidance says. Checking on vulnerable neighbours, friends and relatives is also advised.

references.title: NHS inform: Heatstroke and heat illness
GOV.UK: Beat the heat: staying safe in hot weather
British Red Cross: Heatstroke and heat exhaustion first aid for children and babies
NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service: Heatwaves and medicines

sprains-and-strains-treatment-and-recove.name: Sprains and strains: treatment and recovery
sprains-and-strains-treatment-and-recove.headline: Sprains and strains: how they are treated and when it is more than a sprain
sprains-and-strains-treatment-and-recove.summary: The NHS describes PRICE care for the first 2 to 3 days, and most sprains and strains feel better after about 2 weeks.
keyPoints: A sprain is a torn or twisted ligament, while a strain is an overstretched or torn muscle, often called a pulled muscle.
The NHS describes PRICE for the first 2 to 3 days: protection, rest, ice, compression and elevation.
The NHS suggests paracetamol for pain, ibuprofen gel for swelling, and speaking to a pharmacist about the best option.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E after a crack, if the body part has changed shape, or if it is numb, tingling, cold, blue or grey.
NHS 111 is the route the NHS gives for severe or worsening pain, large or growing swelling, not being able to put weight on the injury, or self-care not helping.
Strenuous exercise such as running may need to be avoided for up to 8 weeks because of the risk of further damage.

body.heading: What is the difference between a sprain and a strain?
body.body:
A sprain is an injury to a ligament, one of the tough bands that connect the bones at a joint. The NHS says sprains most often happen in the wrists, ankles, thumbs and knees. A strain is an overstretched or torn muscle, which people also call a pulled muscle. The NHS says strains most often affect the feet, legs and back.

The NHS lists pain, tenderness or weakness, swelling or bruising, difficulty putting weight on the area, and sometimes muscle spasms. A broken bone can cause similar signs, which is why the warning signs later in this guide matter.

body.heading: What does the NHS describe for the first few days?
body.body:
For the first 2 to 3 days the NHS describes five steps known as PRICE. The letters stand for protection, rest, ice, compression and elevation. Rest means stopping exercise or activities and trying not to put weight on the injury.

For ice, NHS trust leaflets describe an ice pack, or a bag of frozen vegetables wrapped in a towel, held on for 15 to 20 minutes at a time every 2 to 3 hours. Several leaflets warn against putting ice directly on the skin. Compression means a bandage that is firm but not too tight, and elevation means keeping the injury raised. The timings vary between sources.

Several NHS trusts also use the word HARM for the first 48 to 72 hours: avoid heat, alcohol, running and massage.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about pain relief and moving the injury?
body.body:
The NHS suggests paracetamol to ease pain and ibuprofen gel to help with swelling. It also says a pharmacist can advise on the best option. The Northern Ireland government site nidirect says ibuprofen should not be taken for the first 48 hours after an injury because it may slow healing, so advice differs between UK sources.

NHS guidance also says to keep the joint or muscle moving once pain allows, so that it does not become stiff. Some trust leaflets describe starting gentle movement early for sprains, while strained muscles are usually rested for at least a few days.

body.heading: When does the NHS say to call 999 or go to A&E?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if there was a crack at the time of the injury. The same applies if the injured body part has changed shape, or if it is numb or tingling. Skin that has turned blue or grey, or feels cold, is also on the list. The NHS says not to drive there; someone else can drive, or 999 can be called for an ambulance.

body.heading: When does the NHS say to get help from NHS 111 or a GP?
body.body:
The NHS lists reasons to get help from NHS 111. These are pain that is very bad or getting worse, and swelling or bruising that is large or growing. Others are being unable to put weight on the injury, an area that is very stiff or hard to move, and self-care that has not helped. A very high temperature, or feeling hot, cold or shivery, can point to infection and leads to the same advice.

NHS 111 Wales says to see a GP if the injury is getting worse or is not feeling better after treating it yourself.

body.heading: How long does recovery take, and when can normal activity restart?
body.body: The NHS says most sprains and strains feel better after about 2 weeks. It adds that strenuous exercise, such as running, may need to be avoided for up to 8 weeks because of the risk of further damage. NHS 111 Wales says severe sprains and strains can take longer than 2 weeks. These timings are general, and recovery that is slower than usual is one reason the NHS gives for seeking advice.

body.heading: Is physiotherapy needed?
body.body: NHS 111 Wales says a GP may refer a person to a physiotherapist if recovery is slower than usual. The main NHS page adds that NHS physiotherapy is not available everywhere and waiting times can be long. A physiotherapist can assess the injury and guide exercises to restore movement and strength.

references.title: NHS 111 Wales - Health A-Z: Sprains and strains
Management of acute injuries (sprains and strains) PRICE guidelines - Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust

nosebleeds-what-helps-and-when-to-get-he.name: Nosebleeds: what helps and when to check
nosebleeds-what-helps-and-when-to-get-he.headline: What helps a nosebleed, and when should it be checked?
nosebleeds-what-helps-and-when-to-get-he.summary: Most nosebleeds can be treated at home by sitting forward and pinching the soft part of the nose, and some need urgent or routine medical checks.
keyPoints: The NHS says most nosebleeds start just inside the nostril, where fragile blood vessels can break easily.
The NHS describes sitting down, leaning forward and pinching the soft part of the nose for 10 to 15 minutes while breathing through the mouth.
The NHS advises going to A&E if bleeding lasts longer than 10 to 15 minutes, seems heavy, or comes with dizziness or difficulty breathing.
The NHS lists regular nosebleeds, a nosebleed in a child under 2, and nosebleeds in people taking blood-clot-preventing medicines such as warfarin as reasons to see a GP.
NHS inform advises spitting out blood that collects in the mouth or throat rather than swallowing it.

body.heading: What causes a nosebleed?
body.body: The NHS says most nosebleeds start just inside the nostril, where the blood vessels are fragile and break easily. NHS guidance lists nose picking and blowing the nose very hard among common triggers. A minor injury to the nose can also cause one.

body.heading: How does the NHS say to stop a nosebleed?
body.body: The NHS describes sitting down and leaning forward, rather than tilting the head back. The soft part of the nose is pinched, just above the nostrils, for 10 to 15 minutes. Breathing is through the mouth during this time. NHS inform advises spitting any blood that collects in the mouth or throat into a bowl rather than swallowing it.

body.heading: When does a nosebleed need A&E or 999?
body.body: The NHS advises going to A&E if a nosebleed lasts longer than 10 to 15 minutes or the bleeding seems heavy. Other reasons it lists include bleeding after a blow to the head, feeling dizzy, and difficulty breathing. The NHS advises against driving to A&E; someone else can drive, or 999 can be called for an ambulance. Some NHS trust leaflets give longer limits, such as 20 minutes, so the exact threshold varies between sources.

body.heading: When should a nosebleed be checked by a GP?
body.body: The NHS lists regular nosebleeds as a reason to make a GP appointment. It also lists nosebleeds in people taking medicines that prevent blood clots, such as warfarin, which are also called anticoagulants. One NHS trust leaflet says people on these medicines whose bleeding does not stop can contact the GP or NHS 111. Leaflets also describe referral to an ear, nose and throat (ENT) department when nosebleeds keep coming back.

body.heading: What about nosebleeds in children?
body.body: The NHS lists a nosebleed in a child under 2 as a reason for a GP appointment. Red Cross first-aid guidance for children describes sitting up and leaning forward, not tilting the head back, so blood does not run into the airway or stomach. It describes pinching the soft part of the nose and breathing through the mouth, with blood spat out rather than swallowed. A children's hospital leaflet advises A&E if bleeding goes on longer than 20 minutes despite first aid, a longer limit than the NHS page gives for adults.

body.heading: What treatment might a hospital offer?
body.body: NHS inform says treatment may include ointments for the nose, cautery to seal blood vessels, or nasal packing. Hospital leaflets describe cautery as using a silver nitrate stick when bleeding continues.

body.heading: What helps after a nosebleed has stopped?
body.body: NHS trust leaflets advise avoiding hard nose blowing for a time afterwards, and sneezing with the mouth open if needed. The same leaflets avoid hot drinks for a period, though they differ on how long, from about a day up to a few days. They also differ on nose blowing, with advice ranging from avoiding forceful blowing to up to a week.

references.title: Learn first aid for a child who has a nosebleed - British Red Cross
Nosebleeds - Alder Hey Children's Hospital Trust
Nosebleeds - The Dudley Group NHS Foundation Trust

anaphylaxis-and-adrenaline-auto-injector.name: Anaphylaxis and adrenaline auto-injectors
anaphylaxis-and-adrenaline-auto-injector.headline: Anaphylaxis: what it is and what the NHS says about adrenaline auto-injectors
anaphylaxis-and-adrenaline-auto-injector.summary: Anaphylaxis is a severe allergic reaction; the NHS describes adrenaline, calling 999 and hospital care, and says people at risk usually get two auto-injectors.
keyPoints: Anaphylaxis is a severe allergic reaction in which the immune system overreacts to a trigger, often a food, a medicine or an insect sting.
The NHS lists swelling of the throat and tongue, fast or difficult breathing, feeling faint or dizzy, and blue, grey or pale skin or lips as signs.
The NHS describes using an adrenaline auto-injector straight away if the person has one, then calling 999 and saying they think it is anaphylaxis.
The NHS says a person who has had a severe reaction or been given adrenaline should always be taken to hospital, because symptoms can come back.
NHS inform says people at risk are usually prescribed two auto-injectors, and MHRA guidance covers carrying two, checking expiry dates and brand-specific training.

body.heading: What is anaphylaxis and what triggers it?
body.body:
Anaphylaxis is a severe allergic reaction. NHS inform describes it as the immune system overreacting to a substance that is usually harmless, which prompts the release of chemicals such as histamine. The NHS treats it as a medical emergency.

Common triggers named in NHS material include certain foods, some medicines and insect stings, such as wasp or bee stings. NHS inform adds that the cause is sometimes never found.

body.heading: What symptoms does the NHS describe?
body.body:
The NHS lists swelling of the throat and tongue, difficulty breathing or breathing very fast, and feeling faint or dizzy. It also lists skin, lips or tongue turning blue, grey or pale.

Resuscitation Council UK guidance says skin or mucosal changes on their own, without airway, breathing or circulation problems, do not mean anaphylaxis. The same guidance says skin changes can be absent in up to a fifth of cases, so their absence does not rule it out.

body.heading: What does the NHS describe as emergency treatment?
body.body:
The NHS says to use an adrenaline auto-injector if the person has one and the helper knows how to use it correctly. It then advises calling 999 for an ambulance and saying the person may have anaphylaxis. This applies even if they start to feel better.

On position, the NHS describes lying the person down with their legs raised, unless breathing difficulty means they need to sit up. A pregnant woman is described as lying on her left side. If an insect stinger is stuck in the skin, the NHS describes removing it.

The NHS says that if symptoms do not improve after 5 minutes and a second auto-injector is available, another injection can be given. Some hospital leaflets give a different timing, so the NHS wording is the one followed here. MHRA guidance says that when there is doubt about the severity of an episode, adrenaline should be given without delay.

body.heading: Why is hospital care needed afterwards?
body.body:
The NHS says a person who has had a severe allergic reaction, or has been given adrenaline, should always be taken to hospital for further observation and treatment. Symptoms can come back after the first treatment, which doctors call a biphasic reaction.

The NHS treatment page describes hospital care that can include oxygen and fluids given into a vein. Resuscitation Council UK guidance says there is no reliable way to predict who will have a second reaction, so decisions about discharge are made for each person by an experienced clinician.

body.heading: Who is prescribed adrenaline auto-injectors?
body.body:
NHS inform says people at risk of anaphylaxis are usually prescribed two adrenaline auto-injectors. The most common brands it names are EpiPen, Jext and Emerade.

MHRA guidance on the GOV.UK site says people prescribed these devices should carry two at all times. It also says to check expiry dates and obtain replacements before they run out, because an expired device is expected to be less effective, and a pharmacist can help with replacements.

body.heading: What practical points do the MHRA and NHS raise?
body.body:
The MHRA says technique varies between auto-injector brands, so people with allergies and their carers should be trained on the particular device they have been prescribed. Manufacturers can supply training pens that contain no adrenaline, and regular practice with these is recommended.

The MHRA guidance also refers to carers. It says carers, as well as the person with the allergy, should be trained on the specific device prescribed.

body.heading: What happens after a reaction?
body.body:
NHS inform says that after anaphylaxis a person may be referred to an allergy clinic, which gives advice and medication to help prevent further reactions. The NHS says blood tests may be done in hospital to help confirm anaphylaxis.

Resuscitation Council UK guidance states that everyone who presents with anaphylaxis should be referred to an allergy clinic to look for the cause, with an adrenaline auto-injector offered in the meantime unless a medicine caused the reaction.

references.title: Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis: guidelines for healthcare providers - Resuscitation Council UK
Adrenaline auto-injectors (AAIs): new guidance and resources for safe use - GOV.UK

travellers-diarrhoea-avoiding-and-managi.name: Avoiding and managing travellers' diarrhoea
travellers-diarrhoea-avoiding-and-managi.headline: How travellers can avoid diarrhoea, and what the NHS says helps if it happens
travellers-diarrhoea-avoiding-and-managi.summary: Travellers can lower the risk of diarrhoea with careful food, drink and hand hygiene, and replacing lost fluid is the main way it is managed.
keyPoints: Travellers' diarrhoea is loose, frequent stools that start during or soon after a trip, usually from eating or drinking something contaminated.
Careful hand hygiene and food and water precautions are the main ways to lower the risk, though TravelHealthPro notes they do not give full protection.
The main aim in treatment is to replace lost fluid, and a pharmacist can suggest oral rehydration powder.
Loperamide can be bought without a prescription by people aged 12 and over, but TravelHealthPro advises against it when there is blood or mucus in the stool, a high fever or severe tummy pain.
Medical help is advised for blood or mucus in the stool, a high fever, signs of dehydration, or symptoms that do not improve within three days.

body.heading: What is travellers' diarrhoea and why does it happen?
body.body:
Travellers' diarrhoea is a bout of loose, watery stools that happens during a trip or shortly after it. It usually comes from swallowing germs in contaminated food or water. For most people it is unpleasant but mild and settles without specific treatment.

The NHS says diarrhoea in adults and children usually stops within 5 to 7 days, and any vomiting usually stops in 1 or 2 days. The NHS covers diarrhoea and vomiting together, since stomach bugs such as norovirus often cause both.

body.heading: What food and drink habits help avoid it?
body.body:
TravelHealthPro advises choosing food that is freshly prepared, fully cooked and served hot. NHS 111 Wales gives similar advice, suggesting salads and uncooked fruit and vegetables are best skipped unless the traveller has washed and peeled them.

Where tap water may not be safe, NHS 111 Wales recommends filtered or bottled water and advises against ice in drinks. Boiled water, hot drinks made with it, and bottled fizzy drinks with intact seals are described as generally safer choices.

body.heading: How does hand washing fit in?
body.body:
TravelHealthPro and Fit for Travel describe good hand hygiene, along with food and water precautions, as central to prevention. Washing hands with soap and water, for example before eating, is the usual method.

Even with careful hand washing and food and water preparation, travellers' diarrhoea remains a common travel-related illness. These precautions lower the risk but do not remove it, so TravelHealthPro advises travellers to be prepared to manage symptoms during a trip.

body.heading: What helps once diarrhoea has started?
body.body:
The NHS says the key step is to drink plenty of fluids, in small, frequent sips if feeling sick. A pharmacist can advise on oral rehydration powder, which replaces lost salts and sugars. TravelHealthPro notes that the water used to make it up should be safe.

The NHS says it is fine to eat when able to, and that fruit juice and fizzy drinks can make diarrhoea worse.

body.heading: Can loperamide or other medicines help?
body.body:
Loperamide is an anti-diarrhoeal medicine, and the NHS says a pharmacist can recommend it for short-term diarrhoea. The NHS says it can be bought without a prescription by anyone aged 12 or over, while younger children need a prescription.

The NHS lists blood in the stool and a high temperature as reasons not to take it. TravelHealthPro goes further, advising against loperamide when there is blood or mucus in the stool, a high fever or severe abdominal pain. It also advises against it for anyone with active inflammatory bowel disease.

body.heading: When should a traveller get medical advice?
body.body:
TravelHealthPro says medical care should be sought if symptoms have not improved within three days. It advises immediate medical care for a high fever, or for blood or mucus in the stool. Older people, children and other vulnerable travellers are advised to seek medical advice earlier if they cannot keep fluids down or show signs of dehydration.

The NHS lists feeling thirsty, headache, feeling light-headed, dark yellow strong-smelling urine and peeing less often among the signs of dehydration. It also lists a dry mouth and sunken eyes. The NHS says an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 is advised for signs of serious dehydration, such as unusual tiredness, dizziness that does not pass on standing, dark yellow urine or peeing less than usual, or fast breathing or heartbeat. For signs of shock, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E, and not to drive.

references.title: NHS: Who can and cannot take loperamide
TravelHealthPro: A food and water hygiene reminder for travellers
NHS 111 Wales: Food and water abroad

malaria-prevention-for-travellers.name: How travellers can reduce malaria risk
malaria-prevention-for-travellers.headline: Malaria and travel: the ABCD approach, bite prevention and when to seek help
malaria-prevention-for-travellers.summary: UK guidance sums up malaria prevention as ABCD: awareness of risk, bite avoidance, antimalarial tablets where needed, and prompt diagnosis.
keyPoints: UK guidance describes an ABCD approach to malaria: awareness of risk, bite avoidance, chemoprophylaxis (antimalarial tablets) where appropriate, and prompt diagnosis.
Malaria is passed on by the bite of an infected mosquito, and the NHS lists DEET-based repellent and insecticide-treated nets among the ways to avoid bites.
The NHS says travellers heading to an area where malaria is found can get advice from a GP, nurse, pharmacist or travel clinic before they go.
TravelHealthPro says no antimalarial tablet is completely effective, but taking tablets together with bite avoidance gives substantial protection.
The NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or getting help from NHS 111 if malaria symptoms follow travel, and UK guidance says malaria can appear up to a year after a trip.

body.heading: What is malaria and how is it caught?
body.body:
Malaria is an illness caused by a parasite. The NHS says it is spread by the bite of an infected mosquito.

The NHS says symptoms usually appear between 7 and 18 days after a bite. Sometimes symptoms do not appear for months after travel, and rarely not for years.

body.heading: What does the ABCD approach mean?
body.body:
UK guidance describes an ABCD approach to preventing malaria in travellers. A stands for awareness of risk, which includes checking whether a destination carries malaria risk. B stands for bite avoidance.

C stands for chemoprophylaxis, the medical term for antimalarial tablets taken to prevent infection where they are appropriate. D stands for diagnosis, meaning that anyone with symptoms gets medical help promptly.

body.heading: How can mosquito bites be avoided?
body.body:
The NHS advises using a DEET-based insect repellent on the skin and sleeping under an insecticide-treated mosquito net. UK guidance on bite avoidance also describes covering exposed skin.

The NHS also says there is no scientific evidence that electric buzzers, savoury yeast extract, tea tree oil, bath oils, garlic or vitamin B protect against bites.

body.heading: Who gives advice about antimalarial tablets?
body.body:
The NHS says travellers heading to an area where malaria is found can get advice from a GP, nurse, pharmacist or travel clinic before they go. UK government guidance says to seek this advice in plenty of time, and that it is never too late to ask.

The GOV.UK chemoprophylaxis guidance compares tablets. It reports that people taking mefloquine are more likely to report abnormal dreams, trouble sleeping, anxiety and low mood than those taking atovaquone-proguanil or doxycycline.

body.heading: Do the tablets give complete protection?
body.body:
TravelHealthPro says no antimalarial tablet is 100% effective, but taking tablets together with mosquito bite avoidance gives substantial protection. Its guidance for people visiting friends and relatives says tablets are started before travel and continued as directed.

GOV.UK says people who have visited or lived in a country with malaria before do not have the same protection as local residents.

body.heading: What are the symptoms of malaria?
body.body:
The NHS lists a high temperature or feeling hot, cold and shivery, sweating, headaches, confusion, muscle pains, and yellow skin or whites of the eyes (jaundice). It also lists feeling very tired and sleepy, especially in children.

The NHS says jaundice may be less noticeable on brown or black skin.

body.heading: Who should be contacted if symptoms appear after travel?
body.body:
The NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or getting help from NHS 111 if there are symptoms after travel to a country where malaria is found. NHS 111 Wales applies this to travel in the last 12 months.

UK guidance says malaria can develop up to a year after a trip. It advises telling the doctor about the travel. The NHS says anyone who travelled with the person should also get help straight away.

references.title: GOV.UK: Malaria, health advice for travellers
TravelHealthPro: Travelling to visit friends and relatives

burns-and-scalds-first-aid-and-when-to-g.name: Burns and scalds: first aid and when to get help
burns-and-scalds-first-aid-and-when-to-g.summary: Cooling a burn under running water for 20 minutes is the first step; the NHS says large, deep, facial, chemical or electrical burns need A&E or 999.
keyPoints: The NHS says a burn should be cooled with cool or lukewarm running water for 20 minutes as soon as possible after the injury.
NHS advice is never to use ice, iced water, creams or greasy substances such as butter on a burn, and not to burst blisters.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for a burn that is very large or deep, is on the face or genitals, or is caused by a chemical or electricity.
For children, the NHS says that, depending on how severe the burn or scald is, the choice is a GP, a minor injuries unit or A&E.
The NHS says small burns and scalds usually close in about two weeks, and that a wound not healed after two weeks needs urgent advice from a GP or NHS 111.

body.heading: What is the difference between a burn and a scald, and how are they sized?
body.body: Burns are skin damage from dry heat such as fire or a hot object, and scalds are skin damage from hot liquid or steam. NHS-linked guidance describes a minor burn as affecting the outer layers of skin, which look red or pale pink, slightly swollen and painful. Deeper burns that cause white or charred skin are described as needing emergency assessment. A burn the size of the person's hand or bigger is described by the Healthier Together service as an emergency. Blistering at the burn site is also listed as a reason to seek urgent help for a child.

body.heading: What first aid does the NHS describe?
body.body: The NHS describes cooling the burn with cool or lukewarm running water for 20 minutes, starting as soon as possible after the injury. Clothing or jewellery near the burn is described as taken off, but anything stuck to the burnt skin is left in place because removing it could cause more damage. After cooling, the NHS describes covering the burn with cling film laid in a layer over it, rather than wrapped around a limb. NHS 111 Wales adds that a clean, clear plastic bag can be used for a burn on the hand. For a child, the NHS describes keeping the child warm and avoiding ice or very cold water, which can make the wound worse.

body.heading: What should be avoided, and what helps with the pain?
body.body: The NHS says never to use ice, iced water, or any cream or greasy substance such as butter on a burn. Blisters will burst naturally, and the NHS advises against bursting them because this can cause infection. For pain, the NHS suggests paracetamol or ibuprofen, following the maker's instructions on the packet. It adds that children under 16 should not be given aspirin.

body.heading: Which burns need A&E or a 999 call?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for a burn that is very large or deep. The same applies to a burn on the face, genitals or bottom, and to a burn caused by an acid, a chemical or electricity. The NHS also says not to drive to hospital, and to ask someone else to drive or to call 999 for an ambulance. NHS treatment guidance also says to go to A&E if someone has been injured on purpose or if that is suspected. Healthier Together guidance adds burns on the neck, hands, feet or any joint to the list needing urgent assessment. Breathing in smoke can cause delayed symptoms such as coughing, a sore throat, difficulty breathing or singed nasal hair, and these still need A&E. Where a burn is smaller and less deep, the NHS says it can often be treated at home.

body.heading: What about chemical and electrical burns?
body.body: For a chemical burn, the NHS acid and chemical burns page lists calling 999 first. It then describes removing contaminated clothing, brushing off dry chemicals and flushing the area with cool or lukewarm running water for about an hour. The NHS says treatment for these burns happens in hospital, where painkillers, antibiotics and fluids into a vein may be given. A burn caused by electricity is also in the NHS list of burns needing 999 or A&E. Burn network guidance gives longer rinsing times for some chemical burns, so the duration is not the same in every source.

body.heading: What about children and babies?
body.body: For a child, the NHS describes putting the burn or scald under cool running water for 20 to 30 minutes straight away. It then says to see a GP, or go to a minor injuries unit or A&E, depending on how severe the burn or scald is. Where there is no running water, the NHS child page describes using cold water or another cool fluid such as milk.

body.heading: How does a burn heal, and what are the signs of infection?
body.body: The NHS says how long a burn takes to heal depends on how serious it is and how it is treated. Minor, superficial burns usually close in about two weeks, while deeper burns can take months or longer. The NHS advises urgent medical advice from a GP or NHS 111 if the wound has not healed after two weeks. The NHS Recovery page lists a wound that becomes painful or smelly, a high temperature, or a dressing soaked with fluid as other reasons for urgent advice. Hospital patient leaflets add spreading redness, swelling, warmth and discharge as possible signs of infection. The South West Burns Clinical Network says a burn not healed in this time can carry a risk of sepsis.

references.title: NHS: What to do if your child has an accident

choose-the-right-nhs-service-999-111-gp-.name: Which NHS service to use: 999, 111, GP, A&E
choose-the-right-nhs-service-999-111-gp-.headline: Choosing between 999, NHS 111, a GP, a pharmacy and urgent care
choose-the-right-nhs-service-999-111-gp-.summary: The NHS says 999 is for life-threatening emergencies and NHS 111 for urgent problems or when unsure, with pharmacies, GPs and urgent treatment centres for others.
keyPoints: The NHS advises calling 999 for life-threatening emergencies, such as a suspected heart attack, a suspected stroke or severe bleeding.
NHS 111 can be used online, in the NHS App or by phone, at any time, when help is needed urgently but the situation is not life-threatening, or when it is unclear where to go.
The NHS says a pharmacist can help with a minor illness, and in England the Pharmacy First service covers seven common conditions without a referral.
Urgent treatment centres give urgent help when a problem is not life-threatening, for example for sprains and strains, suspected broken bones or skin infections.
If it is unclear where to go, the NHS suggests using NHS 111 first, which will advise where to go for treatment.

body.heading: How do the NHS urgent care services differ?
body.body: The NHS has several services for different levels of need. The NHS says 999 is for life-threatening emergencies. NHS 111 is for urgent problems that are not life-threatening, or for when a person is unsure where to go. Urgent treatment centres give urgent help when a problem is not a life-threatening emergency. For less urgent health needs, the NHS says to contact a GP or a pharmacist in the usual way. A pharmacist can help with a minor illness.

body.heading: When does the NHS say to call 999?
body.body: The NHS says 999 is for life-threatening emergencies. Examples in NHS guidance include loss of consciousness, an acute confused state, chest pain, breathing difficulties and cardiac arrest. Further examples include fits that are not stopping, a suspected stroke, severe bleeding, severe allergic reactions, severe burns or scalds, serious head injuries and major trauma. The NHS advises calling 999 for a heart attack or a stroke. Hospital emergency departments, often called A&E, are the place for serious emergencies.

body.heading: What does NHS 111 do?
body.body: NHS 111 is for medical help that is needed urgently when the problem is not life-threatening. It can be used online at 111.nhs.uk, in the NHS App, or by phone. It is available 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, and calls are free from landlines and mobile phones. The online service is for people aged 5 and over. The NHS says to call 111 instead for a child under 5, for complex problems caused by an existing medical condition, for people with a care plan from their doctor for the current problem, or for end-of-life care.

body.heading: What happens when someone calls NHS 111?
body.body: The NHS says the call starts with basic questions, such as who is calling, where they are, and whether the problem affects the caller or someone else. The adviser then asks about the symptoms, including when they started and what has already been tried, as well as any medicines being taken and any existing medical conditions. These questions are there to rule out a life-threatening condition first. The NHS says the call does not give a diagnosis, but it does tell the person what help they need. The outcome may be an ambulance, a referral to urgent care, a GP or another service, or advice on looking after the problem at home. If a nurse is due to call back, the NHS says someone needs to be available to answer.

body.heading: What can a pharmacist help with?
body.body: The NHS lists seeing a pharmacist for help with a minor illness as an option for less urgent needs. In England, the Pharmacy First service lets people use seven pathways by contacting or visiting a pharmacy directly, without a referral. The seven conditions are sinusitis, sore throat, earache, infected insect bites, impetigo, shingles and uncomplicated urinary tract infections. Each has its own age range, so not everyone is eligible. NHS England says the pharmacist assesses the person privately, advises on self-care and, only if appropriate, supplies a limited set of prescription-only medicines. If the pharmacy cannot help, the person is directed to a GP surgery or A&E as appropriate.

body.heading: What do urgent treatment centres and GPs do?
body.body: The NHS says urgent treatment centres give urgent medical help when it is not a life-threatening emergency. They can help with problems such as sprains and strains, suspected broken bones, stomach pain, vomiting and diarrhoea, skin infections and rashes, and a high temperature. Some centres also offer tests such as an ECG, blood tests or an X-ray. A GP registration is not needed to attend. NHS England sets a national standard of opening at least 12 hours a day, seven days a week, with both booked and walk-in patients seen. Appointments can be booked through NHS 111. For less urgent needs, the NHS says to contact a GP in the usual way.

body.heading: What if it is not clear where to go?
body.body: When it is unclear which service fits, the NHS suggests calling 111 first. The NHS says NHS 111 will assess the problem and may offer the chance to speak to a nurse, doctor or paramedic. The person is then advised where to go for treatment. What a local urgent treatment centre offers can vary, so tests and opening arrangements may differ between areas. If someone appears to be in a life-threatening situation, the NHS advises calling 999.

references.title: NHS: When to use NHS 111 online or call 111

blood-clots-on-long-flights-dvt-risk.name: Long flights and DVT: risk and how to lower it
blood-clots-on-long-flights-dvt-risk.headline: Can long flights cause blood clots (DVT), and what reduces the risk?
blood-clots-on-long-flights-dvt-risk.summary: Long journeys can raise the chance of a leg blood clot (DVT); the NHS and TravelHealthPro describe moving, drinking water and sometimes stockings.
keyPoints: A deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is a blood clot in a deep vein, usually in the leg, and a clot that reaches the lungs is called a pulmonary embolism.
Sitting still for long periods is one of the risk factors the NHS lists, and TravelHealthPro names groups of travellers at higher risk who are advised to seek advice from a health professional.
Walking about, doing calf exercises, drinking water and wearing loose clothes are among the steps described for journeys; sources differ on how widely compression stockings are advised.
For suspected DVT the NHS says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111, and to call 999 or go to A&E for sudden difficulty breathing or chest pain.
Treatment is usually with anticoagulants, often called blood thinners, which aim to keep the clot from growing while the body gradually breaks it down.

body.heading: What is DVT, and how can it affect the lungs?
body.body:
A deep vein thrombosis, or DVT, is a blood clot in one of the deep veins, most often in the leg. The NHS says the main worry is that part of the clot can travel to the lungs. This is called a pulmonary embolism, and the NHS lists it among the reasons to call 999.

Some clots cause no symptoms at all, which is why a DVT can be hard to spot.

body.heading: Why are long journeys linked to blood clots?
body.body:
Blood flow in the leg veins slows when the legs stay still. The NHS lists being immobile, such as sitting or lying down for long periods, among the things that raise the risk of DVT. The NHS also says that on journeys of four hours or more by plane, train or car, there are things that can lower the chance of DVT.

TravelHealthPro, the UK national travel health service, has a factsheet on venous thromboembolism, the term covering DVT and pulmonary embolism together.

body.heading: Who is at higher risk?
body.body:
TravelHealthPro lists a previous DVT or pulmonary embolism, a family history of clots, a clotting disorder, recent surgery or injury, cancer, pregnancy and being overweight as factors that raise the risk of travel-related clots. It says travellers at increased risk are advised to seek advice from their health care provider.

The NHS DVT page also lists cancer, hormone replacement therapy and the oestrogen-based contraceptive pill among the things that raise the chance of DVT.

body.heading: What can lower the risk on a long journey?
body.body:
NHS 111 Wales travel advice describes walking around when it is possible, and doing calf and ankle exercises while seated. It also describes drinking water, avoiding alcohol and wearing loose, comfortable clothes.

On stockings, the sources differ. NHS 111 Wales says passengers who wear compression stockings on flights of four hours or more can significantly reduce their risk of DVT and leg swelling, and that ill-fitting ones could raise the risk. TravelHealthPro advises travellers at increased risk to consider properly fitted below-knee graduated compression socks. An NHS cancer alliance information sheet for GPs is more cautious: it says routine use of stockings or anticoagulants for all travellers is not recommended, and that stockings are for those at the highest risk.

body.heading: What are the symptoms, and who should be contacted?
body.body:
The NHS describes a throbbing pain and swelling in one leg, usually in the calf or thigh. The skin over the area can look red, blue or darkened, and the veins near the surface can be swollen.

For suspected DVT, the NHS says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111. The signs of a pulmonary embolism include sudden difficulty breathing, chest pain that is worse when breathing in, and coughing up blood. The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for sudden difficulty breathing, chest or upper back pain, a very fast heartbeat or passing out. It advises against driving yourself to A&E, and says to ask someone to drive or call 999 for an ambulance.

body.heading: How is DVT treated?
body.body:
Treatment usually involves anticoagulants, often called blood thinners. Their main role is to keep the clot from growing while the body gradually breaks it down. Hospital leaflets note that anticoagulants increase the risk of bleeding, so people taking them are told to report unusual bleeding.

Doctors choose the medicine and how long treatment lasts for each person, and the leaflets advise talking to a doctor before stopping it.

travelling-with-medicines-what-the-nhs-s.name: Travelling with medicines: what the NHS says
travelling-with-medicines-what-the-nhs-s.headline: Planning, packing and paperwork for medicines when travelling, as the NHS and TravelHealthPro describe
travelling-with-medicines-what-the-nhs-s.summary: The NHS and TravelHealthPro describe original packaging, hand luggage, a prescriber's letter and checking the rules of each destination country.
keyPoints: TravelHealthPro, whose medicines advice is also published on nhs.uk, describes keeping medicines in original pharmacy packaging, with a copy of the prescription and a prescriber's letter.
The same guidance describes carrying medicines in hand luggage, with some extra supply in the hold luggage.
TravelHealthPro says a prescriber's letter listing generic medicine names can help at border checks and if medicines need replacing or medical help is needed.
GOV.UK says that, when leaving the UK with medicine containing a controlled drug, a person should be able to show the medicine is theirs.
TravelHealthPro discourages obtaining insulin overseas, because names, brands, strengths and quality vary widely around the world.

body.heading: How should medicines be packed and carried?
body.body: TravelHealthPro describes keeping medicines in their original pharmacy packaging. It advises carrying a copy of the prescription and a letter from the prescriber. The same guidance describes carrying medicines in hand luggage, with some extra supply in the hold luggage. TravelHealthPro also says airline rules should be checked, particularly for liquids, because limits apply to the amount that can be carried in hand luggage. It adds that travellers should check that their medicines are permitted in the countries they will visit.

body.heading: What does a letter from the prescriber do?
body.body: TravelHealthPro suggests asking the prescriber for a letter that lists the medicines by their generic names. Generic names are the official names of the active ingredients, rather than the brand names on the box. TravelHealthPro says such a letter can be helpful during border control checks. It says the letter can also help if medicines need replacing or medical help is needed. Home Office advice on controlled drugs describes a letter that gives the traveller's name, the travel dates, the destination and the medicines with their quantities.

body.heading: Can liquid medicines go in hand luggage?
body.body: Airport limits on liquids in hand luggage can affect liquid medicines. NHS 111 Wales says essential medicines in amounts of more than 100ml can be taken in hand luggage with approval arranged in advance with the airline and airport. It says a letter from a doctor or a prescription should be carried as well. Because airline rules differ, TravelHealthPro advises checking them ahead of travel.

body.heading: What applies to controlled drugs and country rules?
body.body: Controlled drugs are medicines that are covered by drug laws, such as morphine, diazepam and codeine. GOV.UK has a page on travelling with medicine that contains a controlled drug. It also has a separate page on bringing such medicine into the UK. GOV.UK says that, for leaving the UK, a person should be able to prove the medicine is theirs, with a prescription or a letter from the clinician. GOV.UK describes personal licences for some controlled drugs, which are applied for through the Home Office. GOV.UK says the rules in other countries can differ, so the embassy of the country to be visited can be contacted. It warns that travelling with a medicine that is illegal in another country could lead to a fine or prison.

body.heading: What do the sources say about insulin?
body.body: TravelHealthPro advises carrying insulin in hand luggage, because it may freeze in the aircraft hold. It discourages obtaining insulin overseas. The reason given is that the names, brands, strengths and quality of insulin vary considerably around the world.
